stemMd: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: Recording custom in a statute changed how legal disputes were settled and shifted authority towards professional interpreters.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Writing a custom down preserves it unchanged, as the communes’ contemporaries believed.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Medieval jurists drafted statutes obscurely in order to make themselves indispensable as interpreters.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The northern Italian communes abandoned customary law within two generations of writing their statutes.

explanationMd:
A central-claim question is answered by the shape of the whole passage, not by any one sentence.

Trace the structure. Paragraph 1 states the thesis: writing custom down "selects, abridges and freezes it, and in doing so it changes what the custom is." Paragraph 2 supplies the mechanism: fixed words mean a hard case is settled by interpretation rather than by shared recollection, and the interpreter — a trained jurist — gains an authority the oral system gave no one. Paragraph 3 supplies the evidence: the clauses subordinating statute to custom, and their disappearance as "the older authority had been absorbed by the newer one." Option B is the only choice that covers both halves of that argument — the change in how disputes are settled *and* the shift of authority.

**How to check.** Ask of each option: could the passage have been written to support this? A good central-claim answer should make most of the paragraphs look like support for it. Options that a single sentence supports, or that no sentence supports, are details or inventions rather than the main point.

distractorRationale.b: This is the view the passage attributes to contemporaries — "the statutes, they said, merely recorded what everyone already knew" — and then rejects. Mistaking a reported view for the author’s own is the most common error on central-claim questions; look for the sentence that turns against it, here "Modern historians are more sceptical."
distractorRationale.d: The passage says the *clauses* referring to ancient custom largely disappeared within two generations, not that customary law itself was abandoned. This option overstates a single detail from the last two sentences and promotes it to the status of the main point.
distractorRationale.c: Nothing in the passage attributes a motive of this kind to anyone. The author says the drafters "seem to have half-understood" what they were doing, which is close to the opposite of a deliberate scheme, and the jurists in the passage interpret statutes rather than draft them.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying history passage, asking which of four statements best expresses the passage’s central claim.

provenance.notes: Original item written against an original passage.

review.author: bocconi-law-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The passage argues that writing custom down 'changes what the custom is' (para 1) and that hard cases are then settled by interpreting fixed words, giving the trained jurist 'an authority that the oral system never conferred on any single person' (para 2) - exactly B. A is the contemporaries' view the author rejects; C overstates (the subordination clauses disappeared, not customary law); D imputes a motive never asserted.
